strategy.summary:
Drehzentrum Ilzauer is a small founder-owned turning shop with stable finances. It is under-utilised: the second shift has been on hold since spring, it advertises free capacity and it has paused hiring. It is also short of cash and openly unhappy about our chronic late payment. We are about a sixth of its turnover and an important reference customer for it. The owner admits his costing is stale and delegated to the office manager.

The three parts behave differently:
- Shaft sleeve 320020 and spacer sleeve 320090 (stainless, dual-sourced, our tooling): history strongly favours us; it asks small increases and settles at zero or below.
- Shaft sleeve 320020: the latest quote is an extreme outlier that no driver supports. It is most likely a costing or unit error.
- Wear ring 320040 (CuSn10, single source): copper has risen sharply, which gives the supplier a real cost case. This is our weak spot, and quality on this part is the worst of the three.

Our best currencies are on-time or faster payment, more volume and a longer commitment, not squeezing. Quality and delivery fall short of targets and are legitimate counter-arguments. Evidence on margin is thin: there is no should-cost for any part.
strategy.decision_maker: The founder-owner decides personally, in meetings and on relationship grounds. The office manager prepares the costing, so figures in quotes come from that office and may be outdated or wrong.

price_view.reasoning:
Stainless sleeves 320020 and 320090:
- Drivers justify only a few percent and history settles at zero or below.
- The 320020 quote is an obvious error to be reset near the current price.
- 320090 at flat is already a good result.

Wear ring 320040:
- The copper rise is real and the part is single-sourced, so a moderate increase or a copper clause is likely fair.
- Aim to absorb part of it with volume, payment and length.

Overall: there is no should-cost, so any judgement of margin is thin. We are a large share of its turnover, so do not crush it.

do: Acknowledge our late payment openly and offer punctual or faster payment as a genuine fix
Thank it for the reference-customer relationship and its cooperation (returnable packaging)
Treat the 320020 figure as a probable error and ask it to recheck, without accusing it
Pair every price step with a volume, length or payment trade and a fresh verified record
Address the owner personally and frame proposals as filling his capacity
dont: Do not threaten to move volume or terminate
Do not ridicule its stale costing
Do not complain about its delivery while ignoring our own late payment
Do not demand long payment terms from a cash-short shop
Do not ask open questions about its cost structure

traps: Accepting or countering near the 320020 outlier quote: reset it to the current price instead of splitting the difference.
Citing peak-based indices (index_peak args): they are not checkable and cost trust.
Citing rival order prices: this reveals the rivals' prices, and they are higher anyway, so it helps the supplier.
Rival quotes from the earlier RFQs were higher than its own, so citing them hurts us.
The single-source position on 320040 and its sound balance sheet: pushing past a final offer risks it walking away.
Asking for longer payment: it contradicts its cash need and our late-payment record.
Using the market copper news or the copper index change ourselves: both support its case.
Promising faster payment that Finance cannot deliver: it would deepen the grievance.
strategy.writer_notes: Open each negotiation with recognition of the partnership and a concrete answer on payment: punctual payment now, faster payment as an offered trade. Treat each part differently. - Ask it to recheck, and anchor at the current price with a modest driver-based allowance. - Offer a larger quota share conditional on better delivery. - Offer binding volume, a two-year term and possibly a copper clause in exchange for a smaller fixed step. - Seek a ppm commitment. Save faster payment for the closing round. Hold one fresh record for each later round.

findings.text: No should-cost exists for any of the three parts, so we cannot say how far its prices sit above full cost. Price room can only be judged from index movements, price history and rival prices. The evidence on margin is thin.

Part 320020 shaft sleeve: the new quote of EUR 30.03 is +158% on the current EUR 11.66. The weighted driver changes justify only about +3.8% (LCI +0.90%, PPI-C2431 +2.33%, AS-14404 +0.83%, power -0.15%), which is roughly EUR 12.10. Nothing in the indices supports the quote; it looks like a costing error, which fits the owner's own admission that his costing is out of date. The rival sup:70230 is paid EUR 12.06 and is approved with a 40% quota, and we own the tooling.

Part 320090 spacer sleeve: the quote of EUR 4.60 is flat against the current price, even though weighted drivers point to about +4% (bars +12.3%). Its price fell 4.8% since 2023 and the rival is paid EUR 4.64. There is little room to push lower; accepting flat is already a good result.

Part 320040 wear ring set (CuSn10, single source): copper is +47.7% in 12 months at a 30% weight, so about +14.3%, plus labour about +0.85%. That gives the supplier a real case for roughly +15% (about EUR 15.6). Its price has risen only 8.5% since 2023. This is the part most exposed to a justified increase, and an index clause on copper may be raised.

The stainless and energy drivers are past their peaks: AS-14404 is -13% from its 36-month peak and -5.5% since 2026-06, PPI-C2431 is -2.3% since 2026-06, and power is -3.7% over 12 months. Recent momentum for the inox parts is down, but only the 12-month and within-12-month changes are checkable.

Contract clause 3.1 fixes prices per calendar year and requires 90 days' notice before year end. A September quote can only take effect in 2027. The supplier also values faster payment (we pay late on average), which is a trade it wants.

findings.text: Small founder-owned turning shop (20 staff, 2-5 M EUR turnover). The owner decides and meets us in person, but costing is delegated to an office manager. On two separate visits the owner admitted he has not tracked his material and energy prices since the 2022 peak. Expect owner-level decisions driven by relationship and gut feel rather than a tight cost model. Any increase request is likely built on stale figures.

It is under-utilised and wants work. The second shift has been on hold since spring 2026. It is publicly advertising free machine capacity, has paused hiring and told us it could take additional parts at short notice. Volume, extra parts or bundling are its strongest needs.

Cash matters to it, and our late payment is a real grievance. On 2026-05-05 it asked for payment within 10 days against a cash discount. On 2026-05-15 it complained that invoices are overdue again and threatened to 'review our conditions'. Our record supports the complaint: we pay 10.3 days late on average, 96.8% of invoices are late, 45% are more than 10 days late, the maximum is 28 days, and 7 invoices are unpaid. This is our main sensitivity. Paying on time or faster, or using its discount offer, is a cheap trade that gives it what it needs.

We matter to it. It twice called Hollerau an important reference customer, and our FY2026 spend of about EUR 569k is about 16% of its turnover. Recognition and the reference status are levers. Being a key account for it also means we must not push it into distress.

Its finances are stable, not distressed. Equity ratio is 40.8%, the credit index is unchanged at 249 and the audit grade is B. The free capacity and cash-discount request point to utilisation and liquidity pressure, but there is no sign of insolvency risk. It could walk away if treated badly.
Its performance weakens its position. Quality is 1000 ppm against a peer median of 457 ppm, with 2 overdue 8D reports. On-time delivery is 84.4% against a 95% target.

It takes a cooperative operational stance, for example switching to returnable packaging from November 2025. Its renewal history shows asks of +3 to +5% that settle near 0% on parts 320020 and 320090.

findings.text: Framework agreement runs 2025-07-01 to 2027-06-30 and covers all three parts. Prices are fixed per calendar year. Any change needs written notice at least 90 days before year end, so for 2027 the deadline was about 2026-10-02. A 2027 increase raised after that has no contractual basis. Payment is 30 days net (our standard is 60), delivery EXW with a 28-day lead time, OTD target 95%, and a EUR 150 flat fee per supplier-caused complaint.
The contract auto-extends by 12 months unless terminated with 90 days' notice, i.e. by 2027-04-01. That exit is still open and credible because we own the tooling on all three parts.

History on stainless sleeves (320020, 320090) favours us. The supplier asked about +1.5% on average and settled about -1.4%. The last renewals asked +3.0% and +3.3% and both settled at 0. The price trend since 2023 is -3.6% and -4.8%.

The bronze wear ring (320040) is different. It is single-sourced at 100% quota with no RFQ ever held. The supplier won increases there: +5.2% settled against +6.6% asked, and +3.1% against +5.2%, giving +8.5% since 2023. The gap is only about 1.8 pp. Copper is up about 48% in 12 months, so expect a large ask; this is our weak spot.

Sourcing differs by part. On 320020 we hold 60% with Lindlbauer at 40%. On 320090 the split is 50/50 with Fuchsreiter. The 2025 benchmark RFQs on both were won by Ilzauer, so rivals quoted higher, about +10-11%. Rival current order prices are only +3.4% and +0.9% above Ilzauer's, so a shift threat on price alone is weak, but a volume shift is feasible.

The supplier is a small founder-owned firm (20 staff). Our spend is about EUR 569k, roughly 16% of its turnover. It advertises free capacity, has its second shift on hold, and calls us a reference customer. Its dependence on us is high.

Our own weakness on payment: we pay on average 10 days late against a 30-day term. The supplier has complained and threatened to review conditions, and it asked for 10-day payment with a cash discount. Cash is its main need and our best trade currency.

findings.text: Delivery is persistently weak: rolling OTD 84.4% (85.7% vs confirmed) against a 95% contract target, roughly at peer median 84.6%, and down from 86.8% a year earlier. When late, it averages 21.1 days late in the last 12m (15.8 all-time), max 41. The gap to target is the argument; the peer comparison does not hurt them much.

Spacer sleeve 320090 is the delivery problem part: 76.9% on time, 23.1% late, avg 23.5 days late, max 41. Sleeve 320020 is at 88% and wear ring 320040 at 88.5%. A second source (sup:70250) carries 50% of 320090 at a near-identical price, so volume can shift.

Quality deteriorated from 565 ppm (2024Q3) to a peak of 1227 ppm (2026Q1); it is now 1000 ppm, roughly 2x the peer median of 457. The trend is slightly improving from the peak. Two 8Ds are overdue, and 5 QNs from Jul-Sep 2026 are still open without d8.

Wear ring 320040 (CuSn10, single source, 100% quota) drives the defects: 1288 ppm last 12m, 25 supplier-caused QNs over the full QN history, mainly coating, leakage and porosity. It is also the only part whose price rose: 12.53 to 13.59 (+8.5%). Paying more for worse quality is a strong point for us; copper +47.7% is their strong counterpoint.

On shared parts it is worse than the rival on quality: 320020 at 521 ppm vs 391 for sup:70230; 320090 at 797 ppm vs 318 for sup:70250. It is cheaper on both parts, though: 11.66 vs 12.06 and 4.60 vs 4.64.
The EUR 150 flat fee recovers little: about 0 to 150 per QN, with many QNs at 0. The true cost of defects is likely understated.

Volume outlook is up on all three parts and has been shared with them: 320020 21910 vs 19160 ordered; 320040 31600 vs 27940; 320090 27000 vs 25080. Combined with their free capacity, this volume is a trade currency for price and ppm commitments.

Their side of the case: we pay late (avg 10.3 days after due) and they have asked for faster payment, giving them a legitimate grievance. Order-side delivery data is otherwise clean: qty variance 0.08% and confirmations matching requests in the latest POs.

arguments.text: Wear ring 320040 is CuSn10 bronze and copper is our dominant material cost: the copper notation is at a 36-month peak, about +48% year on year. With copper at roughly 30% of the part cost, that alone is around +14% on cost, while we settled only +3.1% for 2026. We need a real increase on 320040 or a copper index clause.

Stainless bar and processing costs are up. Cold-drawn bar prices are +12.3% in 12 months, the 1.4404 alloy surcharge is +6%, steel is +7.3% since January and labour is +2.7%. Over three rounds we accepted zero or below on 320020 and 320090, so we have absorbed this for years.

Your late payment is costing us financing. 96.8% of invoices are paid late, on average 10.3 days past due in the last 12 months and up to 28 days late. We hold your price fixed while carrying your credit.

We are already cheaper than the second sources: 11.66 vs 12.06 on 320020 and 4.60 vs 4.64 on 320090. We also won both 2025 benchmark RFQs. The 4.60 quote on 320090 is a flat rollover, which is a concession in itself.
We are the only qualified source for 320040, and we have delivered reliably at 88.5% on time in the last 12 months on that part.

weak_points: The 320020 quote of 30.03 is indefensible: about +158% with no cost driver behind it, and our owner admitted our costing is stale. We must withdraw it quietly as a costing error before it costs us credibility on everything else.
We have idle capacity: the second shift has been on hold since spring, we advertise free capacity and we have paused hiring. The customer knows we need the volume.
Quality is poor. Overall ppm has run about 1,000-1,227 against 391 and 318 at the competitors. On 320040 ppm is 1,288, and two 8D reports are overdue.
Delivery is weak: on time only about 84% against a 95% target, and only 76.9% on 320090, with delays of up to 41 days.
Energy prices are down 43% on 2022 and down 3.7% year on year.
Hollerau is about a sixth of our turnover and we called it an important reference customer twice.
Both stainless parts are dual-sourced with customer-owned tooling, so share can shift to Lindlbauer or Fuchsreiter.
Our evidence is thin: no should-cost exists, and our own costing is not current.
wants: Payment within 10 days, or at least strict adherence to 30 days net; we would grant a cash discount or a price concession in return.
A binding annual volume and higher quota shares on 320020 and 320090 to refill the second shift.
Additional parts to fill free capacity.
An extension of the contract to 24-36 months for planning security.
A copper index clause on 320040 instead of a fixed price.
red_lines: No fixed-price reduction on 320040 without copper protection.
No price decreases on the stainless parts without volume or payment in return.
We will not accept continued late payment while the price stays fixed.
No ppm penalty or chargeback above the current flat EUR 150 per complaint while copper costs are this high.
red_team.opening: Correct 320020 to roughly 12.0 (+3%) and call the earlier quote a costing error. Hold 320090 flat at 4.60. Ask about +8% on 320040 to about 14.7, or a copper index clause on the current base. Tie everything to punctual payment and offer a cash discount for payment within 10 days. Signal openness to a longer commitment and more volume. Keep the tone cooperative and respectful.

rebuttals.answer: You are right that copper has risen sharply and that this is a real cost on the wear ring; we take it seriously. Copper is one part of the cost, not all of it, and the wear ring is also the one part where the price has already risen every year since we started buying it. We would rather share the risk transparently than fix a large step at a peak: a copper clause or a moderate fixed step, combined with the higher volume we now forecast and a two-year term, gives you protection and planning security. We would also want the open complaints on this part closed out as part of the package.

Bar prices have risen, and we accept that this is a genuine driver. Weighted by their share of the part cost, however, the stainless drivers support only a small change: the alloy surcharge has fallen back recently and electricity is lower than a year ago, which offsets part of the rise. That points to a modest adjustment at most, and certainly nothing near the new shaft sleeve figure, which we assume reflects a costing slip and would ask you to recheck.

You are right, and we apologise: our payments have been late too often, and that is not acceptable. We will commit to paying on the agreed terms. We are also open to taking up your own proposal of payment within ten days against a cash discount, which helps your liquidity directly and can be reflected in the price.

We value that your prices on the sleeves are competitive and that you won both benchmarks; that is exactly why we want to keep and grow the business with you. Competitiveness is measured on total cost, though. On both sleeves your complaint rate and on-time delivery trail the second source, so the gap in unit price narrows once quality and delivery are counted. A flat rollover on the spacer is a fair result, and we would happily reward better delivery with a larger share.

We appreciate being able to rely on you for the wear ring, and we own the tooling for it. On-time delivery on this part has improved, but it still falls short of the target in our agreement. Complaints on this part are the highest of the three, and several reports are still open. A price step on the wear ring needs to go hand in hand with a clear quality commitment.

We would like to understand your plan for bringing on-time delivery up to the target in our agreement, especially on the spacer sleeve.
